title: Shooting inquiry begins today: Officer shot immigrant twice in neck: [Final Edition 1]
article: A long-awaited public inquiry into the police shooting death of a 34-year-old Sudanese immigrant will be beneficial for the city, says a member of the local Sudanese community.
The scheduled eight-day fatality inquiry into the Oct. 25, 2003, death of Deng Fermino Kuol begins today before provincial court Judge Gerald Meagher.
"It's for everybody in the city, not just our community, to know what happened," said Andre Ding, one of 7,500 members of the New Sudanese Community Association in Calgary.
"It's good for both sides, the family of the person who died and the officer. Maybe the officer will be found innocent and it will be good for his psychological well-being."
Kuol, who was intoxicated, died from two gunshot wounds to the neck after police answered a call about a disturbance in the 1700 block of 37th St. S.E. shortly after midnight.

Kuol, who escaped wartorn Sudan and moved to Canada in 1997, allegedly attacked Const. Ira Macumber, 41, with a knife. Police say he slashed Macumber in the arm before the officer reacted in self- defence.

Macumber, a four-year member of the force, was later cleared of wrongdoing. It followed an investigation by the city police homicide unit and reviews by the department's professional standards section and the Edmonton special Crown prosecutor.
The judge cannot find fault, but can make recommendations to help prevent similar incidents from occurring in the future.

Kuol's family members could not be reached for comment. However, when the inquiry was announced last winter, his cousin Lith Akau said police should re-examine the policy on use of deadly force in such confrontations.
"I want to know exactly what happened and I want the Justice Department to give out the right answers," Akau said at that time. "I'm glad there is an inquiry."
Last month, during a pre-inquiry conference, Alberta government lawyer Nancy McCurdie advised Meagher that the Calgary Police Service policy on deadly force will be a key issue.

McCurdie, who will be co-counsel with Jo-Ann Burgess, said the other key questions to be answered were whether the fatal outcome would have been different if a second officer had been on scene, and whether all satisfactory communication was made prior to the shooting.
